[ i ]Preface Welcome to Blender 3D: Characters, Machines, and Scenes for Artists! Blender 3D is one of the top pieces of 3D animation software. Machine modeling is an essential aspect of war games, space games, racing games, and animated action films. As the Blender software grows more powerful and popular, there is a demand to take your modeling skills to the next level. Let your creative freedom begin! What this learning path covers Module 1, Blender 3D Cookbook , will take you on a journey to understand

the workflow normally used to create characters, from the modeling to the rendering stages, using the tools of the last official release of Blender exclusively. With the help of this module, you will be making production-quality 3D models and characters quickly and efficiently, which will be ready to be added to your very own animated feature or game. Module 2, Blender 3D Incredible Machines , will help you develop a comprehensive skill set that covers the key aspects of mechanical modeling. Through

this module, you will create many types of projects, including a pistol, spacecraft, robot, and a racer. By the end of this module, you will have mastered a workflow that you will be able to apply to your own creations. Module 3, Blender 3D By Example , will help you to create many types of projects using a step-by-step approach. Each project in this module will give you more practice and increase your knowledge of the Blender tools and Blender game engine. EBSCOhost: eBook Collection (EBSCOhost)

CAD sketch primitives: line (2 points), circle (center+radius), arc (3 points or center+angles), rectangle (2 corners), ellipse (center+2 radii+rotation), spline (control points).
Sketch constraints hierarchy: first fix position (coincident to origin), then orientation (horizontal/vertical), then size (dimensions), then relationships (equal, parallel, tangent).
Sketch best practices: start from origin, use construction lines for reference, dimension fully (no under/over-constrained), use symmetry when possible, keep sketches simple.
Common sketch patterns for mechanical parts: bolt circle (circle + radial pattern of holes), keyway (rect on circle), gear tooth (involute curve), thread profile (triangle/trapezoid).
Sketch-to-3D workflow: draw profile → add constraints → add dimensions → verify fully constrained → extrude/revolve/sweep/loft → add features (fillet, chamfer, hole).

SketchGraphs dataset: 15 million CAD sketches from Onshape. Each sketch is a constraint graph where nodes are geometric entities and edges are constraints. Most common entities: lines (45%), arcs (20%), circles (15%).

Most common constraint patterns in real CAD sketches: coincident (35% of all constraints), horizontal/vertical (25%), dimension/distance (20%), tangent (8%), equal (5%), perpendicular (4%), parallel (3%).
Sketch complexity distribution: median sketch has 8 entities and 12 constraints. Simple parts use 3-5 entities. Complex parts may have 50+ entities per sketch. Multiple sketches per part is common.
Parametric design patterns: use named dimensions for key values, link dimensions with expressions (hole_diameter = shaft_diameter + 0.1), use configurations for variants.
Constraint solver behavior: under-constrained sketches have degrees of freedom (entities can move). Over-constrained sketches are invalid (conflicting rules). Fully constrained is ideal.
Common sketch topologies: closed profiles (for extrude), open profiles (for sweep path), construction geometry (reference lines/points), centerlines (for revolve axis).

Mechanical part design workflow: 1) Understand requirements (dimensions, material, loads). 2) Sketch main profile. 3) Extrude/revolve base feature. 4) Add secondary features (holes, fillets, chamfers). 5) Pattern repeated features. 6) Shell if needed. 7) Add cosmetic features (emboss, thread).

Common mechanical parts and how to model them: Shaft (circle → extrude), Gear (polygon → extrude → circular pattern teeth), Bracket (L-shape → extrude → holes → fillet), Housing (rect → extrude → shell → holes), Spring (helix → sweep circle along path).

Sheet metal design rules: minimum bend radius = material thickness, K-factor 0.33 for steel, bend allowance BA = angle × (radius + K × thickness), flat pattern length = sum of flat lengths + bend allowances.
Injection molding design rules: uniform wall thickness 1-4mm, draft angle 1-3 degrees on vertical walls, rib thickness = 0.5-0.7 × wall thickness, avoid undercuts, gate location at thickest section.

3D printing design rules: minimum wall thickness 0.8mm FDM / 0.3mm SLA, overhang angle max 45° without supports, bridge length max 10mm, minimum hole diameter 2mm, layer height affects surface finish.
Assembly design: use mate connectors for precise positioning, ground the base part, add mates in order (most constrained first), check interference, create exploded views for documentation.
Gear design formulas: module m = pitch_diameter / teeth_count, addendum = m, dedendum = 1.25m, tooth_thickness = π×m/2, center_distance = m×(teeth1 + teeth2)/2, pressure_angle = 20° standard.
Fastener selection: M3 for electronics, M4-M5 for light mechanical, M6-M8 for structural, M10+ for heavy duty. Socket head cap screw most common. Bolt length = grip + 1.5 × diameter.
Tolerance stack analysis: worst case = sum of all tolerances. Statistical (RSS) = sqrt(sum of squares). Bilateral tolerance ±0.1 means 0.2 total range. H7/g6 for sliding fit, H7/p6 for press fit.
CAD file formats: STEP (universal exchange), IGES (legacy exchange), STL (3D printing, triangles only), OBJ (simple mesh), GLTF/GLB (web 3D), DXF/DWG (2D drawings), Parasolid (Onshape/NX native).

Most populated: table (8,443), car (7,497), chair (6,778), airplane (4,045), sofa (3,173), rifle (2,373), lamp (2,318), vessel/boat (1,939), bench (1,816), loudspeaker (1,618). All models are polygon meshes with textures. Free for research.

ABC Dataset CAD model statistics: average model has 50-500 faces, 100-2000 edges, 50-1000 vertices. Common features: fillets (78% of models), chamfers (34%), holes (62%), extrusions (95%), patterns (21%). Most models are mechanical parts: brackets, housings, gears, shafts, connectors.

ABC Dataset design patterns: most common feature sequence is sketch→extrude→fillet (45% of models), followed by sketch→extrude→hole→fillet (23%), sketch→revolve→fillet (12%). Average model has 4.7 features. Simple parts: 2-3 features. Complex: 10-20 features.

Simple character modeling in CAD: Head = sphere (radius 1). Body = cylinder (radius 0.8, height 3). Arms = cylinders (radius 0.25, height 2.5). Legs = cylinders (radius 0.35, height 3). Hands = spheres (radius 0.3). Feet = boxes (0.3x0.15x0.5). Use fillets at joints for smooth transitions.

Stylized character proportions (chibi/cartoon): 2-3 heads tall. Head = 1/2 to 1/3 total height. Large eyes (1/3 of face). Small body, short limbs. Big hands/feet relative to limbs. Exaggerated features for expressiveness.

Standard bolt/screw dimensions (metric): M3 (3mm shaft, 5.5mm head, 2.4mm socket), M4 (4mm, 7mm, 3mm), M5 (5mm, 8.5mm, 4mm), M6 (6mm, 10mm, 5mm), M8 (8mm, 13mm, 6mm), M10 (10mm, 16mm, 8mm). Thread pitch: M3=0.5, M4=0.7, M5=0.8, M6=1.0, M8=1.25, M10=1.5.

Bearing dimensions (common): 608 (8x22x7mm skateboard bearing), 6001 (12x28x8mm), 6201 (12x32x10mm), 6202 (15x35x11mm), 6203 (17x40x12mm), 6204 (20x47x14mm). Inner ring = shaft diameter. Outer ring = housing bore. Press fit: shaft h6, housing H7.

Gear modeling: spur gear profile is involute curve. Simplified: use polygon with teeth_count sides, extrude, then boolean-subtract the dedendum circle. Module = reference diameter / teeth. Addendum = module. Dedendum = 1.25 × module. Tooth thickness at pitch circle = π × module / 2.

Common mechanical assemblies: Motor mount (L-bracket with 4 holes), Shaft coupling (cylinder with keyway and set screws), Pulley (cylinder with V-groove, center bore), Clamp (C-shape with bolt hole), Hinge (2 leaves with pin hole), Linear rail (T-slot extrusion).

Spring design: compression spring OD = wire_dia × (spring_index + 1), where spring_index = 4-12 typical. Free length = solid_height + deflection + clearance. Wire diameter from load: d = sqrt(8 × F × D / (π × τ)), where τ = shear stress, D = mean diameter.

Residential window types and sizes: casement (600-1200mm wide, 600-1500mm tall), double-hung (600-900mm wide, 900-1800mm tall), sliding (1200-3000mm wide), fixed picture (900-2400mm wide), awning (600-1200mm wide, 300-600mm tall). Sill height: 900mm standard, 300mm for floor-to-ceiling.

Roof construction in CAD: flat roof = rect extruded 300mm above walls. Gable roof = draw triangle on side (YZ) plane, extrude width of house. Hip roof = more complex, use loft between rectangle (base) and smaller rectangle (ridge). Pitch: 4:12 to 12:12 typical. Overhang 300-600mm.

Door types and modeling: hinged single (900x2100mm, swing 90°), hinged double (1600x2100mm), sliding (1200-2400mm, parallel to wall), pocket (disappears into wall), bifold (closets, 600-900mm per panel), French (1400x2100mm with glass panels), garage (2400-5000mm wide x 2100-2400mm tall).

Design for Manufacturing (DFM) principles: minimize part count, design for multi-use, design for ease of fabrication, avoid tight tolerances unless necessary, use standard components, minimize assembly directions, design for top-down assembly.

TRIZ inventive principles for design: segmentation, taking out, local quality, asymmetry, merging, universality, nesting, counterweight, preliminary anti-action, preliminary action, beforehand cushioning, equipotentiality. Used to solve engineering contradictions.

Golden ratio (1.618) in design: rectangles with sides in golden ratio are visually pleasing. Applied to: product proportions, UI layout, logo design. Fibonacci spiral derived from golden rectangles. Common in nature: shells, flowers, hurricanes.

Ergonomic design dimensions: desk height 720-760mm, monitor distance 500-700mm, keyboard height 650-700mm, mouse at same height as keyboard, chair seat height 400-520mm adjustable, armrest 180-250mm above seat, lumbar support at 200-250mm above seat.

PROFESSIONAL CAD DESIGN WORKFLOW — 8 PHASES: Phase 1: REQUIREMENTS — Define what the part does, dimensions, material, loads, interfaces. Phase 2: CONCEPTUAL SKETCH — 2D hand-sketch or rough digital sketch of the design intent. Multiple concepts. Phase 3: DETAILED 2D DRAWING — Proper orthographic views (front/top/side), dimensioned, toleranced. Phase 4: 3D MODELING — Build parametric CAD model following sketch-to-feature workflow. Phase 5: ANALYSIS — Check interference, mass properties, FEA stress if needed. Phase 6: ASSEMBLY — Mate parts together, verify motion, check clearances. Phase 7: DOCUMENTATION — Engineering drawings with GD&T, BOM, assembly instructions. Phase 8: EXPORT — Output for manufacturing (STEP for CNC, STL for 3D print, DXF for laser).

PHASE 1 — REQUIREMENTS CHECKLIST: Before modeling, answer: What is this part for? What are the critical dimensions? What material? What manufacturing process (CNC, 3D print, injection mold, sheet metal)? What interfaces with other parts (bolt holes, mating surfaces)? What loads/forces? What environment (temperature, moisture, UV)? What quantity (1-off prototype vs mass production)? What tolerances are needed? What surface finish? Output: A requirements list with dimensions, material, and constraints.

PHASE 2 — CONCEPTUAL SKETCH RULES: Draw 2-3 different concepts before committing to one. Use simple shapes: rectangles for blocks, circles for cylinders, triangles for trusses. Mark critical dimensions with question marks (to be determined). Show how parts interface with each other. Identify the main 'base feature' — the largest/most important shape that everything else attaches to. Note which features are structural vs cosmetic. In GestureCAD: use construction lines (press Q) for reference, draw rough outlines, don't dimension yet.

PHASE 3 — 2D DRAWING STANDARDS (ASME Y14.5 / ISO 128): Third-angle projection (US/UK): front view shows most detail, top view above front, right view to the right. First-angle projection (Europe): front view, top view below, right view to the left. Every dimension must appear exactly once. Place dimensions on the most descriptive view. Use center lines for cylindrical features. Show hidden lines as dashed. Title block: part name, number, material, scale, date, drawn by, checked by, approved by. In GestureCAD: use Drawing tab → Generate 3-View for automatic orthographic views.

PHASE 4 — 3D MODELING BEST PRACTICES: Rule 1: Start with the base feature — the largest/most defining shape. Rule 2: Add features in order of importance (structural first, cosmetic last). Rule 3: Fully constrain every sketch before extruding. Rule 4: Use named dimensions for key parameters (not magic numbers). Rule 5: Fillet/chamfer edges LAST (they're hardest to edit). Rule 6: Use patterns instead of copying features manually. Rule 7: Keep sketches simple — one profile per feature when possible. Rule 8: Use construction geometry for reference (center lines, symmetry lines).

FEATURE ORDER STANDARD (bottom to top of feature tree): 1. Base sketch + extrude (main body shape). 2. Secondary sketches + extrude/cut (pockets, bosses, ribs). 3. Holes (through-holes, counterbores, tapped holes). 4. Patterns (bolt circles, vent patterns, teeth). 5. Shell (if hollow part). 6. Draft (if injection molded). 7. Fillets (round edges — do these LAST). 8. Chamfers (beveled edges). 9. Cosmetic features (emboss text, logos). WHY: Fillets/chamfers are topology-dependent. If you add them early and then change the base, they break.

PHASE 5 — ANALYSIS CHECKLIST: 1. Mass properties: is the weight acceptable? Center of gravity where expected? 2. Interference check: do parts collide? Is there clearance for assembly? 3. Wall thickness: no areas thinner than minimum for manufacturing process. 4. Draft analysis: all vertical faces have sufficient draft for mold release (1-3°). 5. Undercut check: any features that prevent mold from opening? 6. FEA (if needed): apply loads, check von Mises stress < yield strength / safety factor. In GestureCAD: use Simulate tab for stress/thermal/modal analysis.

PHASE 6 — ASSEMBLY WORKFLOW: 1. Ground the base part (the part that doesn't move — frame, housing, etc). 2. Insert parts one at a time, starting with the most constrained. 3. Use mate connectors on faces/edges/vertices for precise positioning. 4. Revolute mate for rotating parts (hinges, gears, wheels). 5. Slider mate for linear motion (drawers, pistons). 6. Fastened mate for bolted connections. 7. Check interference after each part is mated. 8. Create exploded view for assembly documentation. 9. Generate BOM (Bill of Materials) from assembly.

PHASE 7 — ENGINEERING DRAWING CHECKLIST: Every drawing must have: title block, scale, projection symbol, revision. Dimension every feature: lengths, diameters, angles, positions. Add tolerances to critical dimensions (H7/g6 for fits, ±0.1mm for general). Add GD&T where needed: position for hole patterns, flatness for mating surfaces, perpendicularity for alignment. Add surface finish symbols (Ra values): 0.8μm for bearing surfaces, 1.6μm for mating, 3.2μm for general, 6.3μm for rough. Add notes: material, heat treatment, coating, special instructions. Section views for internal features. Detail views for small features.

WHEN CLAUDE BUILDS A DESIGN, FOLLOW THIS EXACT SEQUENCE: 1. First output a text description of what will be built. 2. List the features in order (base → secondary → holes → patterns → fillets). 3. Output cad-commands block starting with set_plane. 4. Base feature: add_entity for the main profile, then extrude_last. 5. Secondary features: additional sketches + extrudes. 6. Holes: apply_feature type=hole with diameter and depth. 7. Patterns: apply_feature type=linear_pattern or circular_pattern. 8. Fillets LAST: apply_feature type=fillet. 9. Never fillet before all geometry is in place. 10. Always set_plane before drawing on a different face.

DESIGN REVIEW QUESTIONS (ask before finalizing): 1. Can this be manufactured with the intended process? 2. Can it be assembled without special tools? 3. Are all tolerances achievable and necessary? 4. Is the material appropriate for the loads and environment? 5. Is the design as simple as possible? (fewer features = cheaper) 6. Are there standard parts that could replace custom ones? 7. Is the part symmetric where possible? (easier to orient during assembly) 8. Are all sharp edges eliminated? (safety + stress concentration) 9. Is there adequate clearance between moving parts? (0.5mm minimum) 10. Does the feature tree read logically from top to bottom?
